title: Job 5:17–27
context: Job 5:17–27 concludes the first speech of Eliphaz. He tells Job that the man God corrects is happy and urges him not to despise the Almighty’s discipline, for God wounds and binds up. He promises that if Job accepts this correction, God will deliver him from famine, war, slander, and destruction; he will be at peace with the stones and animals of the field, his home will be safe, his offspring many, and he will come to the grave in full age. Eliphaz ends by saying that he and his friends have searched this out and that it is true. His words about God’s discipline echo themes elsewhere in Scripture (compare Proverbs 3:11–12 and Hebrews 12:5–6), and both traditions affirm that God disciplines those he loves. Yet both also note that Eliphaz assumes Job is being corrected for sin, which the book’s opening chapters and the LORD’s verdict in 42:7 do not support.

verses.text: “Behold, happy is the man whom God corrects. Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says the man God corrects is happy, and Job should not despise the Almighty’s discipline. Arminians see a true principle, echoed in Proverbs 3:11–12 and Hebrews 12:5–6, while noting that Eliphaz assumes Job is being disciplined for sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that God disciplines those he loves. Both traditions note that the book’s opening chapters show Job’s suffering was not a correction for sin, and they read Eliphaz’s application as mistaken.

verses.text: For he wounds and binds up. He injures and his hands make whole.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says God wounds and binds up, injures and heals. Arminian readers see a true statement about God’s power to restore, which appears elsewhere in Scripture (compare Deuteronomy 32:39; Hosea 6:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over both affliction and healing. Both traditions read the verse as true in itself and note that it anticipates Job’s restoration in chapter 42.

verses.text: He will deliver you in six troubles; yes, in seven no evil will touch you.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says God will deliver Job in six troubles, and in seven no evil will touch him. Arminians see a promise of protection that is true of God’s care, though Eliphaz makes it conditional on Job’s repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the numerical pattern as a poetic way of saying God delivers in every trouble. Both traditions note that Eliphaz’s promise assumes a simple link between righteousness and safety, which the book complicates.

verses.text: In famine he will redeem you from death; in war, from the power of the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says God will redeem Job from death in famine and from the sword in war. Arminian readers see a picture of God’s protection in danger, a theme found in the Psalms.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s power to save. Both traditions read the verse as part of Eliphaz’s promise, true of God’s ability, while noting that the book shows the righteous are not always spared suffering.

verses.text: You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, neither will you be afraid of destruction when it comes.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says Job will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue and will not fear destruction. Arminians see the promise extending to protection from slander, which is a real form of harm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the promise as part of Eliphaz’s picture of a restored life. Both traditions note the irony that Job is about to suffer from the words of his friends, and they read the verse as Eliphaz’s.

verses.text: You will laugh at destruction and famine, neither will you be afraid of the animals of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says Job will laugh at destruction and famine and will not fear wild animals. Arminian readers see a picture of security and peace for the one who trusts God, which Eliphaz presents as the reward of repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as part of his idealized promise. Both traditions note that this picture of security is true of God’s ultimate purposes, though it does not reflect the immediate experience of every righteous person.

verses.text: For you will be allied with the stones of the field. The animals of the field will be at peace with you.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says Job will be in league with the stones of the field and at peace with the animals. Arminians see a poetic image of harmony with creation, which suggests a restored and fruitful life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing peace and blessing. Both traditions read the verse as part of Eliphaz’s promise, and they note that the stones may refer to fields free from rocks that hinder farming.

verses.text: You will know that your tent is in peace. You will visit your fold, and will miss nothing.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says Job will know his tent is at peace and will find nothing missing in his fold. Arminian readers see the promise of a secure home and possessions, painful in light of Job’s losses (1:13–19).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the irony of the promise to a man who has lost everything. Both traditions read the verse as part of Eliphaz’s picture of restoration, which he links to Job’s repentance.

verses.text: You will know also that your offspring will be great, your offspring as the grass of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says Job’s offspring will be great and as numerous as the grass. Arminians note the pain of this promise for a man who had just lost all his children, and they see Eliphaz speaking without fully grasping Job’s grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the promise as true of God’s ability to bless. The word offspring can also be translated seed. Both traditions note that Job is later given more children (42:13), though not on Eliphaz’s terms.

verses.text: You will come to your grave in a full age, like a shock of grain comes in its season.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says Job will come to the grave in full age, like a shock of grain in its season. Arminian readers see a beautiful image of a life completed in peace, which is a true picture of God’s blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing a fruitful, completed life. Both traditions note that Job does live to a full age (42:16–17), while recognizing that Eliphaz’s reasoning about why is not the book’s.

verses.text: Behold, we have researched it. It is so. Hear it, and know it for your good.”
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says he and his friends have searched this out and it is true, and Job should hear and know it for his good. Arminians see confidence that goes beyond what Eliphaz truly knows about Job’s situation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the closing as overconfident. Both traditions read the verse in light of the LORD’s verdict in 42:7, which shows that the friends did not speak what is right about God, despite their certainty.
